newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters restart talks in bid to settle strike. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters restart talks in bid to settle strike. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]

text.p: United Parcel Service and Teamsters union officials met with the help of a federal mediator on Thursday in an effort to break the deadlock that has produced the biggest strike in the United States in 27 years.
Teamsters President Ron Carey met Dave Murray, chief negotiator for UPS, at a Washington hotel for the first time since Saturday as the strike entered its 11th day.
Federal mediator John Calhoun Wells took part in Thursday's talks, which moved to a hotel near the Labor Department and the Teamsters' headquarters.
Labor Secretary Alexis Herman was also present.
"They are meeting here informally with the secretary. This is not yet the beginning of formal talks," Labor Department spokesman Carl Fillichio (corrects from Sillichio) told reporters.

About 185,000 UPS workers have been on strike since Aug. 4, demanding more full-time jobs for some of the company's many part-time employees. Full-time workers earn $20 an hour on average with full benefits while part-timers get reduced benefits and earn about $11 an hour.

The strike has crippled the nation's largest package delivery company, which says it is losing $300 million a week, and sent thousands of businesses scrambling to ship their goods. In addition to the issue of part-time workers, the two sides differ over changes UPS has proposed for the Teamsters pension fund.
But in a sign that compromise was in the air, UPS Vice Chairman John Alden was quoted Thursday as saying the company might back down on the pension proposals.
Reorganizing the funds "may not be in the final package", he told the Wall Street Journal in an interview. Company officials said they were checking the report.

UPS officials said Wednesday they were willing to discuss all issues but would not go into specifics. They have said their last offer was generous and called for Teamsters' leaders to allow union members to vote on it. Carey has declined.

Herman's spokesman said she would remain available to help the talks. President Bill Clinton has refused to intervene to end the walkout, which labor historians said was the biggest since the postal workers' strike of 1970.
Carey said Wednesday he doubted the meeting would end the strike, which has cost UPS hundreds of millions of dollars.
"While there is no reason for optimism at this point, we will be there, ready to negotiate a reasonable agreement that provides the good jobs that American families need," he said.

When the talks broke off on Saturday, UPS Chairman James Kelly called the Teamster position unrealistic. He said Wednesday the company remained "open and willing to examine all avenues that will help our people get back to work."

Herman met with both sides individually Monday but the two sides hardened their positions on Tuesday, when the AFL-CIO said it would provide loans to cover the $10 million in weekly strike pay for striking sorters, loaders and drivers. UPS warned it would cut 15,000 jobs due to lost business.
In another potential problem for UPS, the head of the union representing the company's pilots said Thursday they might strike near Christmas in a separate dispute.

"A strike could potentially occur close to Christmas," Independent Pilots Association President Robert Miller told a news conference. IPA members are already honoring the Teamsters' strike by refusing to fly UPS planes.
About 2,000 members of the Independent Pilots Association normally work for UPS flying its fleet of 500 aircraft. They had been working without a contract since December 1995.
